method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Definition:** current weight or rate of gain significantly below that expected for age and sex, **or weight has dropped 2 or more major percentile lines.**
claims.source_text: Slow weight gain describes a child or infant whose current weight, or rate of weight gain is significantly below that expected for age and sex, or if weight has dropped ≥2 major percentile lines
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Nutrition is the main driver of growth under 2 years; most cases are inadequate caloric intake.** Causes are commonly multifactorial, with psychosocial stressors often significant, and there is not always a pathological cause.
claims.source_text: Nutrition is the main driver of growth in children under 2 years of age. Most cases of slow weight gain are secondary to inadequate caloric intake … Slow weight gain is commonly multifactorial in origin, with psychosocial stressors often a significant contributor … There is not always an underlying pathological cause for slow weight gain
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Length and head circumference are often preserved initially**, but may be affected if undernutrition is severe or prolonged.
claims.source_text: Length and head circumference are often initially preserved in cases of slow weight gain, but may be affected if severe or prolonged insufficient nutrition
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Expected average weight gain (a guide, not the minimum acceptable):** 0–3 months 150–200 g/week; 3–6 months 100–150 g/week; 6–12 months 70–90 g/week.
claims.source_text: The table below is a guide to the expected average weight gain per week (it is not the minimally acceptable weight gain) 0 to 3 months 150–200 g/week 3 to 6 months 100–150 g/week 6 to 12 months 70–90 g/week
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Under 2 years: WHO growth standards**, correcting for prematurity (under 37 weeks) until 2 years. **2 years and over: CDC charts.** Use syndrome-specific charts (e.g. Down, Turner) where appropriate.
claims.source_text: <2 years of age: WHO growth standards. Correct for prematurity (<37 weeks) until 2 years old ≥2 years of age: CDC growth reference charts Use specific growth charts (eg Down, Turner syndrome) where appropriate
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A healthy, gaining baby may cross down to and track along a lower centile** than their birth weight in the first few months.
claims.source_text: In the first few months of life, a healthy baby who is gaining weight may cross and track along a lower centile than that of their birth weight.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Weight under the 3rd percentile in isolation**, with typical neurodevelopment and no red flags, may still be normal — **monitor over time**; extensive investigation may not be needed.
claims.source_text: Children with isolated less than 3rd percentile weight-for-age, but with typical neurodevelopmental progress and no red flags on clinical assessment may still be within normal limits of growth These children should be monitored over time and may not need extensive investigation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A percentile drop on switching from WHO to CDC charts** is usually a chart artefact, not a true change in growth.
claims.source_text: A drop in percentiles may be observed when switching from WHO to CDC charts This is usually due to differences in the charts rather than representing a true change in growth pattern
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Intake history:** breast or bottle, number and volume/duration of feeds per 24 hours, breast milk supply, **formula preparation**; milk intake per 24 hours in toddlers.
claims.source_text: Intake: breast/bottle, number and volume/duration of feeds per 24-hour period, breast milk supply, formula preparation … Milk intake per 24hr period in toddlers
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine** muscle bulk (buttocks), fat stores (thighs), skin, hair, gums, eyes and nails; development, caregiver–child interaction and **signs of abuse or neglect**; **observe a feed if able.**
claims.source_text: Muscle bulk (buttocks), subcutaneous fat stores (thighs), skin, hair, gums, eyes and nails Developmental level, caregiver-child interactions, signs of abuse or neglect Observe feed if able
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **An otherwise healthy, normally developing child with no suggestive features needs no investigations at first.** Otherwise investigate according to the features elicited.
claims.source_text: For an otherwise healthy and normally developing child with no suggestive features on history or examination, no investigations are necessary at first. … If a particular diagnosis is suggested by the history or examination, investigate according to the features you have elicited
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Urine microscopy and culture — especially under 12 months, as occult UTI can present with slow weight gain.**
claims.source_text: Urine: Urinalysis, microscopy and culture (especially infants <12 months of age, as occult UTI can present with slow weight gain)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bloods to consider:** FBE, ferritin, UEC, TSH, glucose, LFT; **coeliac serology and total IgA** if eating gluten; micronutrients, especially active B12 if malabsorption or restricted diet is suspected.
claims.source_text: Blood: FBE, ferritin, UEC, TSH, glucose, LFT If on solids or feeds containing gluten - coeliac serology and total IgA micronutrients – especially active B12 if suspicion of malabsorption or restricted dietary intake
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stool:** microscopy, fat globules, fatty acid crystals. **Over 12 months:** add ESR and faecal calprotectin.
claims.source_text: Stool: Microscopy, fat globules, fatty acid crystals In children older than 12 months: ESR, faecal calprotectin
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Inadequate intake or retention:** inadequate nutrition, breastfeeding difficulties, **formula preparation error**, restricted diets (including vegan, sensory aversions), cleft palate, persistent vomiting, appetite loss from chronic disease, **solids introduced early (before 4 months) or late (after 6 months).**
claims.source_text: Inadequate caloric intake/retention Inadequate nutrition (breastmilk, formula and/or food) Breast feeding difficulties Error in infant formula preparation Restricted diet eg restriction of food groups or macronutrients, vegan, sensory aversions Structural eg cleft palate Persistent vomiting Appetite loss due to chronic disease Early (<4 months) or delayed (>6 months) introduction of solids
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Psychosocial:** parental mental or chronic illness, poor carer understanding, non-secure attachment, mealtime difficulties, **coercive feeding (including feeding while asleep)**, food insecurity, isolation, missed appointments, substance abuse, **family violence, trauma or neglect**, child protection involvement.
claims.source_text: Psychosocial factors Parental mental illness, disability or chronic illness Poor carer understanding eg language barrier, intellectual disability, limited literacy Non-secure attachment patterns Behavioural disorders Difficulties at mealtimes Coercive feeding (including feeding child whilst asleep) Food insecurity Social isolation Failure to attend appointments Parental substance abuse Family violence Trauma or neglect Current or past child protection involvement
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Poor absorption:** cow milk protein allergy, coeliac disease, pancreatic insufficiency (e.g. CF), chronic diarrhoea, chronic liver disease. **Excess utilisation:** UTI, chronic inflammation, chronic respiratory disease, congenital heart disease, diabetes, hyperthyroidism.
claims.source_text: Inadequate absorption Cow milk protein allergy Coeliac disease (if having gluten containing diet) Pancreatic insufficiency eg Cystic fibrosis Chronic diarrhoea Chronic liver disease Excessive caloric utilisation Urinary tract infection Chronic illness / inflammation Chronic Respiratory disease eg Cystic fibrosis Congenital heart disease Diabetes mellitus Hyperthyroidism
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use a multidisciplinary team.** Management is guided by the contributing factors; **most children are managed as outpatients — consider admission if red flags are present.**
claims.source_text: A multi-disciplinary team approach is highly recommended. … Specific management will be guided by underlying contributing factors Most patients can be managed on an outpatient basis Consider admission if red flag features are present
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the paediatric team** for significant malnutrition, illness or dehydration; failed outpatient management; **concern about abuse or neglect**; significant parental mental health concern.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team when Significant malnutrition, illness or dehydration Failed outpatient management Concern about potential child abuse or neglect Significant mental health concern in parent
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider transfer** for severe malnutrition, or an underlying cause needing specialist input.
claims.source_text: Consider transfer when Severe malnutrition, underlying cause or contributing factors requiring specialist input
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge with a clear individualised plan:** feeding plan, and follow-up including outstanding investigations.
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when A clear individualised plan is in place that clearly outlines the following: Recommended feeding plan Details of follow up, including any outstanding investigations
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Weigh infants every 1–4 weeks**, depending on concern. **One clinician (often the child health nurse or GP) owns follow-up** and ensures appointments are attended.
claims.source_text: Weight monitoring every 1-4 weeks is usually sufficient in infants, depending on the level of concern. … One clinician should take responsibility for follow up and ensure that appointments are attended. This can often be a child health nurse and/or GP.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Missed follow-up: act to check the child's wellbeing; refer to Child Protection if at risk.**
claims.source_text: If follow up appointments are not attended, action should be taken to ascertain the wellbeing of the child. Refer to Child Protection if considered to be at risk
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Slow weight gain' (Last updated March 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Slow_weight_gain/, retrieved 2026-09-23
